explanation: A trailer or semi-trailer must have all its wheels resting fully on the road surface at all times; driving with a wheel lifted off the ground due to loading or hitching is never permitted because it compromises stability and braking.
Towing more than a single trailer is restricted and requires prior written approval from the Licensing Authority, since multi-trailer combinations pose extra handling and stability risks.

Parking at a bus stop is normally banned to keep it clear for buses; the Sabbath/holiday exception applies only to private vehicles and only as specified on the sign posted at that particular station.

A trailer without its own independent braking system may not exceed 750 kg regardless of the towing vehicle's own weight, since an unbraked trailer that heavy could overwhelm the tow vehicle's stopping power.
The weight recorded in the bill of lading is treated as conclusive documentary proof of the freight's weight for legal and enforcement purposes.
The driver, who is responsible for ensuring the vehicle is loaded within the legal weight limit, must bear the cost of a weighing that reveals an unlawful, irregular weight.
A police officer has the authority to direct a freight vehicle's driver to the nearest weighing station to verify legal compliance with weight regulations.

An officer may hold a vehicle carrying freight unlawfully at the roadside until the load is unloaded or the irregularity is otherwise lawfully resolved, since an unsafely loaded vehicle should not continue driving.
Oversize freight must always be marked, regardless of the time of day, because the hazard of an extended load to other road users exists both day and night.
Marking of oversize freight on a moving vehicle is required at all times, not just during specific lighting conditions, since the freight's protrusion is a constant hazard.

The law specifies distinct markings for each end: a white light-reflecting triangle at the front and a white triangle with red reflecting edges at the rear, so oncoming and following traffic can each identify the freight's true extent.
Only companies formally approved as licensed haulage contractors may transport hazardous materials; approval cannot be substituted by driver experience or license class alone.
Loose ash and bulk cement may only be carried in vehicles specially built for that purpose, since ordinary open vehicles cannot contain such fine, wind-scattering materials safely.
A vehicle lacking a separate driver's compartment must have a partition protecting the occupants from being struck by the cargo, particularly during hard braking.
An interchangeable crate is legally defined as a crate, box, or similar container built to be lifted on and off the vehicle using a permanently mounted crane.
A permanent crane is a fixture permanently installed on the vehicle specifically to raise and lower interchangeable crates.

After driving through a flooded section, water reduces friction in the braking system, so the driver must drive slowly while pressing the brake pedal gently and intermittently to dry the brakes and confirm they still respond properly.
A freight container is legally defined as a shipping tank or box fitted with a twist-lock anchor bolt and limited to a maximum width of 250 cm.

Containers longer than 610 cm may only be carried on a semi-trailer, and only as explicitly authorized in that vehicle's registration document, since such long loads require a chassis rated for the extra length.
A freight container must never protrude from the rear of the vehicle, as an overhang at the back creates a collision and load-security hazard for following traffic.
Freight containers require twist locks to be securely fastened to the vehicle; without this fitting, the container cannot be reliably anchored and transport is prohibited.
Perimeter lighting is a yellow lighting system outlining an oversize load, with lamps spaced no more than 100 cm apart so its true outline is visible at night.

The escorting vehicle must display caution oversize-freight signs on its front and on the rear of the freight vehicle, plus a flashing yellow light above the cab, giving both approaching and following traffic clear advance warning.

The escort and the freight vehicle must maintain a distance at which the two can keep each other in constant sight, since there is no fixed metric distance; visual contact is what allows the escort to warn of hazards in time.
On a two-way road the escort vehicle drives ahead to warn oncoming traffic of the wide load approaching, while on a one-way road it drives behind to warn traffic overtaking from the rear.
Every tractor must be fitted with a reverse warning buzzer, since the driver's rear visibility is limited and nearby pedestrians or workers need an audible warning when it reverses.
Bulk freight or any part of it may not rise above the height of the vehicle's side walls or any legally fitted extension ladders or racks, to prevent material spilling onto the road.
A vehicle with an all-up weight of 15,000 kg or less, including its freight, is limited to a maximum overall height of 4 meters under vehicle-dimension regulations.
The law requires that freight be arranged and anchored on the vehicle so that it cannot shift or fall off, independent of whether the total weight itself is within the legal limit.

A commercial vehicle over 3,500 kg carrying 11 or more passengers must display a passengers sign on both the front and back, alerting other road users that it is operating as a passenger-carrying vehicle.

A commercial vehicle over 3,500 kg without a chassis designed for passenger transport may carry at most six passengers in addition to those seated beside the driver, since it isn't structurally certified for more.
A vehicle transporting hazardous materials must be parked at least 400 meters from any residential building or public structure, keeping people at a safe distance in case of a leak or explosion.

When parking uphill on a curbed road, a heavy vehicle's front wheels should be turned toward the center of the road, forward gear engaged, and safety chocks placed behind the rear wheels, so that if it rolls it is steered away from traffic and blocked.

At night, a commercial vehicle over 10,000 kg may not park wherever the local traffic-sign authority has posted a sign prohibiting that vehicle type from parking or waiting there, since such restrictions are set locally via signage rather than a blanket rule.

A vehicle over 3,500 kg standing on an interurban road during lighting-up time must always place a warning triangle and additionally use a portable light or four-way flashers, giving approaching traffic redundant visual warning in the dark.
A vehicle may not stand or park on a road if it is wider than 2.50 meters, since an overly wide stationary vehicle would obstruct the roadway for passing traffic.

A trailer or semi-trailer that has been disconnected from its towing vehicle may not be left standing on the road, because a detached trailer lacks proper lighting and braking connection and becomes a serious hazard.
Commercial vehicles with an all-up weight of 12,000 kg or more are capped at 80 km/h on interurban roads, reflecting the lower speed ceiling set for heavier vehicles regardless of road configuration.
Commercial or work vehicles with an all-up weight of 12,000 kg are subject to their own statutory limit of 50 km/h in urban areas, which a general posted 70 km/h sign cannot override.

A driver forced to travel very slowly because of the freight being carried or the road's steepness, thereby delaying traffic behind, must move onto a paved, traffic-free hard shoulder to let following vehicles pass.

A driver of an oversize-freight vehicle who cannot be overtaken due to road conditions must slow down and, if necessary, pull onto the hard shoulder or even stop, to let the vehicles behind overtake safely.
A semi-trailer is legally defined as a cab unit affixed directly to a trailer, distinguishing it from a rigid single-chassis vehicle or one that merely tows another motor vehicle.
A connected truck is defined as a rigid motor vehicle to which a trailer has been coupled, as distinct from a combination involving a semi-trailer or two motor vehicles towing each other.
When visibility is poor on a two-way road, overtaking is forbidden outright, since the driver cannot be sure the opposing lane is clear far enough ahead to complete the maneuver safely.
A tractor is not permitted to enter a freeway at all, because its low speed and design are incompatible with freeway traffic conditions regardless of daylight or towing status.
Overall length is defined as the distance between the vehicle's most forward point and its most rearward point, including any fixed extensions, not just the chassis or axle span.

Buses excluding minibuses, commercial vehicles, and work vehicles with an all-up weight over 3,500 kg are barred from overtaking another vehicle that is itself already overtaking, since two large vehicles occupying the opposing lane at once creates an extreme hazard.

On a road with at least two lanes in the same direction, commercial and work vehicles with an all-up weight over 10,000 kg must enter an intersection from the rightmost of the two lanes, keeping heavier, less maneuverable vehicles out of the way of general traffic.

A driver of a vehicle carrying more than eight passengers who needs glasses or lenses must carry a spare pair in the vehicle in addition to the ones worn, in case the pair being used is lost or damaged mid-journey.
The obligations and prohibitions that apply to commercial vehicles apply to trucks as well, since a truck falls within the legal category of commercial vehicle for regulatory purposes.
A tachograph is a device with a disc that records time, distance traveled, driving speed, and driver work hours, used to monitor compliance with rest and driving-time rules.
A commercial vehicle is legally defined as a vehicle used or designed to transport freight for hire, in connection with the owner's business or trade.
A taxi driver who needs glasses or another optical aid must carry an extra pair with him whenever driving, so that a lost or broken pair doesn't leave him unable to see properly mid-shift.
The Carrier Service Law establishes that transport services using a commercial vehicle with an all-up weight over 10,000 kg may not be provided without holding a carrier license.
Anyone providing transport services with a commercial vehicle weighing 10,000 kg or more is required to hold a carrier license under the Carrier Services Law.
A carrier license is issued for a period of one year, after which it must be renewed.
Under the Carrier Services Law, a commercial vehicle is one with an all-up weight of 10,000 kg or more, or any vehicle transporting hazardous materials regardless of its weight.
A public minibus driver who requires glasses or lenses must carry a spare pair with him while driving, ensuring he is never left without corrective vision aids affecting his passengers' safety.

On a steep, long descent a driver must shift into a suitably low gear at the very start of the descent, so that engine braking is available throughout rather than only once speed has already built up.

There is a risk that a heavy vehicle's gear may fail to engage while shifting on a steep descent, leaving it briefly in neutral with no engine braking at all, which is why gear changes on descents must be handled carefully.

After coupling a trailer to a towing vehicle, the driver must check that the brakes respond properly before starting to drive, since a faulty connection could leave the trailer's brakes non-functional.

On a steep descent a truck should be driven in an appropriate low gear with its special deceleration mechanisms engaged, using engine braking rather than relying on the service brakes alone to avoid overheating them.

A vehicle fitted with a pneumatic air braking system must have a warning lamp, a warning buzzer, and an air-pressure gauge in the driver's compartment, so the driver is alerted if air pressure drops too low for safe braking.

The stability of a freight-carrying commercial vehicle in a curve depends on its speed, the curve's radius, and the height of its center of gravity, since these together determine how much centrifugal force is generated relative to the vehicle's tendency to tip or skid.
Every taxi is required to be equipped with an ABS anti-lock braking system, since taxis carry paying passengers frequently in varied traffic conditions.

The higher a vehicle's center of gravity, the less stable it is when cornering, since a higher center of gravity increases the tipping and rollover tendency under the centrifugal force generated in a turn.
The pictured sign shows an arrow instructing drivers to continue straight or turn right, while explicitly forbidding a left turn, including a left U-turn, at that point.

A tire's manufacture date is molded and marked directly on the tire itself as a date code, not recorded in any vehicle paperwork, since it is a property of that specific tire rather than of the vehicle.
A truck cab should be connected to a semi-trailer by reversing straight back while both are aligned in a single straight line, ensuring the fifth-wheel coupling engages correctly and safely.

On a slippery road, a connected vehicle or semi-trailer truck risks entering a jack-knife position, where the trailer swings out at a sharp angle relative to the towing unit because the trailer's wheels lose grip and slide.

On an interurban road without a center divider, a commercial vehicle up to 3.5 tons is limited to 80 km/h by default, matching the standard speed table for that vehicle class absent a different posted sign.

A service-route bus may only be parked, other than for loading or unloading passengers, according to what its route license permits, since deviating from the licensed route or stops without authorization is not allowed.

On an urban road a commercial vehicle over 12,000 kg is capped at 50 km/h even if a sign permits a higher speed, because the statutory weight-based limit for heavy vehicles overrides a general posted urban speed sign.

The maximum freight weight a commercial vehicle may carry is the weight specified as permitted in that vehicle's registration document, not a value set independently by the manufacturer or tire supplier.
A trailer is legally defined as a unit whose front part rests on the support surface located behind a cab, distinguishing it from a full trailer that carries its own front axle.
Sand scattered on the road reduces the friction between tires and the road surface, making the vehicle prone to skidding, especially under braking or cornering.
The pictured sign designates a path reserved for bicycles, permitting bicycle entry onto that dedicated path.

A freight container may only be transported on a vehicle if its registration document explicitly states that the vehicle is approved to carry freight containers, since the vehicle's chassis and fittings must be certified for that use.

A commercial vehicle with an all-up weight of 12,000 kg or more must have two red and white rectangular reflective plates mounted on its rear, making the outline of the large vehicle clearly visible to traffic approaching from behind.
Centrifugal force acts on a vehicle while it is driving around curves and turns, pushing it outward from the turning path in proportion to speed and inversely to the curve's radius.
Centrifugal force in a turn increases with the square of the speed, so the most effective way to reduce it is to reduce speed before and through corners and curves.

A driver of a commercial vehicle weighing 10,000 kg or more must take a continuous rest break of at least 7 hours before being permitted to resume work, under the driving-hours rest regulations for heavy-vehicle drivers.

Driving in low gear on a steep descent uses the engine's compression to hold a slow, steady speed without relying continuously on the service brakes, which would otherwise overheat and lose effectiveness.
A driver may never exceed the posted speed limit while overtaking, even briefly, since exceeding the limit is prohibited regardless of the maneuver being performed.
A vehicle's emergency lights, or hazard lights, are the simultaneous flashing of all four turn indicators together, used to warn other road users of a hazard or a stopped or slow-moving vehicle.
The default speed limit for a private passenger car on an urban road, absent any sign stating otherwise, is 50 km/h under the standard speed-limit table.
A driver may never exceed the posted speed limit while overtaking, even to shorten the time spent in the opposing lane, since the speed limit itself is not suspended during an overtaking maneuver.
A vehicle non-use notice takes the vehicle off the road entirely; it may only be driven if the non-use form itself permits a specific trip, such as to a nearby garage, and not otherwise.

Reaction distance depends on both the driver's reaction time and the vehicle's speed, since a slower reaction or a higher speed each independently lengthens the distance traveled before any braking begins.

Reaction distance is the distance the vehicle covers from the moment the driver notices a hazard until they begin to act on it, during which no braking or steering control action has yet taken effect.

The total stopping distance, reaction distance plus braking distance, is always longer than the braking distance alone, since braking distance is only one component of the full distance needed to stop.

When a vehicle ahead signals a left turn on a two-way road, you should assume it may indeed move left and let it do so, since a driver must always account for another vehicle's signaled intentions under the general duty of care.
When visibility is poor, a driver must slow down, adjust speed to match the reduced visibility, and turn on the dipped low-beam headlights so that both the driver and others can see and be seen.

Only a person trained and holding a permit issued by the Ministry of Transportation is authorized to transport hazardous materials, since specialized knowledge of handling and emergency procedures is required.

Transporting hazardous materials requires that both the driver and the vehicle hold the appropriate permits issued by the Licensing Authority, since both the person's training and the vehicle's suitability must be certified.

After hitting a parked vehicle whose owner is absent, the driver must leave a note with personal, vehicle, and insurance details at the scene and report the incident to the police within 24 hours, fulfilling the duty to identify oneself when the other party isn't present.
The distance a vehicle travels from the moment the brake pedal is pressed until it stops increases the faster the vehicle is being driven, since braking distance grows with the square of the speed.
Pressing the clutch pedal disengages the engine from the wheels by disconnecting the drivetrain, allowing gear changes or the vehicle to coast without engine power being transmitted.

Before lifting a vehicle to change a wheel, the driver must ensure by every possible means that the vehicle cannot move, with the parking brake applied, wheels chocked, and gear engaged, since a car rolling off a jack is extremely dangerous.
Third-party insurance is the coverage that pays for damage caused to other vehicles or property, as distinct from coverage for the insured's own vehicle.
